title: Open Codex and give it a practice folder
summary: Start with an empty local folder. Its name and contents give you a simple way to verify where Codex is working.
where: Mac or Windows computer with the signed-in ChatGPT desktop app. Use chatgpt.com/download to obtain it.
On iPad, read along or use an available cloud or Remote task. The desktop folder picker lives on the computer.

actions.title: Create the folder
actions.do: In Finder on Mac, open Documents and choose File → New Folder. On Windows, open Documents in File Explorer and choose New → Folder. Name it AI-Practice.
actions.see: AI-Practice appears inside Documents.
actions.stuck: If a folder with that name already exists, use AI-Practice-2 and follow the same steps.

actions.title: Switch to Codex
actions.do: Open ChatGPT on the computer, sign in and select Codex from the app’s product menu.
actions.see: You see the Codex workspace with a sidebar and a place to start a task.
actions.stuck: If you see a regular chat with the Chat or Work toggle, reopen the product menu. A browser tab and the desktop app have different controls.

actions.title: Attach the folder
actions.do: Use + beside Projects, choose Local, then Next. Name the project Practice. Under Source folders, add AI-Practice and choose Create project. A version offering Open folder directly can open the same folder.
actions.see: The local project lists your practice folder as a source.
actions.stuck: In the file picker, open Documents, select AI-Practice itself, then choose Open or Select Folder. Avoid choosing all of Documents.

actions.title: Verify the location
actions.do: Start a chat in Practice. Type “Show the name of the folder you can read and list the files in it. Make no changes.”
actions.see: The response identifies AI-Practice and no user-created files.
actions.stuck: If it lists unrelated documents, stop there and reopen the project with the narrower folder.

roles: Use a local folder for fictional mail-report examples.
Use a folder containing sanitized scripts or sample exports.
Make a practice app in its own folder.

title: Make and find your first Codex file
summary: A successful first task produces something you can open outside the conversation.
where: Use the ChatGPT desktop app on Mac or Windows. Sign in, select Codex, then open a small practice folder as your local project.

actions.title: Name the output
actions.do: In the project, start a chat and type “Create status.txt in this folder with exactly two lines: Queue checked and Ready to review.”
actions.see: Codex describes or performs a small local edit.
actions.stuck: If it only shows possible text, ask it to write the file to the open local project.

actions.title: Check the file yourself
actions.do: Open the same folder in Finder or File Explorer. Double-click status.txt to view it in a text editor.
actions.see: The file contains two lines, in the requested order.
actions.stuck: If double-click opens the wrong program, use Open With → TextEdit on Mac or Notepad on Windows.

actions.title: Request a small revision
actions.do: Return to the same Codex chat. Type “Change only the second line to Reviewed by owner.”
actions.see: The revised result mentions status.txt.
actions.stuck: If two files now appear, explicitly give the original filename and ask which file was edited.

actions.title: Compare with disk
actions.do: Reopen status.txt or reload the editor. Read both lines.
actions.see: Queue checked remains first and Reviewed by owner appears second.
actions.stuck: If the editor still shows the old version, close its tab without saving the stale text and reopen the file from the folder.

roles: Make a sample runbook note.
Draft a short change handoff.
Edit an instruction shown in an app.

title: Read a changed line before accepting it
summary: A diff shows how a file changed. Use a small Git example to read one removed line and one added line.
where: Open Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app on Mac or Windows. Use an approved practice Git repository with a committed README.md.

To make one locally without Git commands, open GitHub Desktop, choose File → New repository, name it ai-review-practice and select Initialize this repository with a README. Open that repository folder in Codex.

actions.title: Read the baseline
actions.do: Open README.md in Finder or File Explorer and note its first heading. Keep that heading somewhere you can compare.
actions.see: You can identify exactly one line to change.
actions.stuck: If the folder lacks a README, use the initialized practice repository described above.

actions.title: Request the edit
actions.do: In a chat in that folder, type “Change only the first heading of README.md to # Practice Guide. Leave all other lines alone.”
actions.see: Codex reports an edit to README.md.
actions.stuck: If you started in ChatGPT Work, switch to Codex and confirm the repository folder.

actions.title: Inspect the difference
actions.do: Open the task’s changed-files or review pane and select README.md. Use Last turn if earlier changes are also shown.
actions.see: The old heading is removed and # Practice Guide is added.
actions.stuck: If no difference appears, check that the original heading was different and that you are viewing the current local project.

actions.title: Make a review decision
actions.do: If any unrelated line changed, request a revision identifying that line. Open README.md again and compare it to the diff.
actions.see: You can explain the entire edit without publishing it.
actions.stuck: If the view shows a review comment on top of the code, read the comment and then inspect the underlying lines.

roles: Check a changed mail-script threshold.
Review which line of a settings guide changed.
Inspect one small UI edit before committing it.
sources: OpenAI · viewing changes and code reviews

title: Find a cloud task from your iPad
summary: A cloud task runs on an OpenAI-managed computer with a connected repository. Your computer’s Documents folder is a separate place.
where: Use chatgpt.com/codex on desktop, or the Codex cloud area of the signed-in ChatGPT mobile app if available. You need an eligible account and a connected practice repository.

actions.title: Find the cloud workspace
actions.do: Sign in to the intended account. On desktop open chatgpt.com/codex. On mobile open the available Codex cloud task area.
actions.see: You can select or see a cloud environment.
actions.stuck: If only local or Remote chats appear, use the desktop web entry to check the account’s cloud access.

actions.title: Choose the project
actions.do: Open the environment selector and choose the practice repository you are allowed to read. Check its name and branch.
actions.see: The task shows its cloud repository context.
actions.stuck: If the repository is absent, check the connected GitHub account and environment setup with its owner. A local folder selection does not upload it.

actions.title: Try a reading task
actions.do: Enter “Read README.md. Return its first heading and the path you used. Leave the repository unchanged.” Start the task.
actions.see: The task has its own progress view and should eventually produce a heading and path.
actions.stuck: If README.md is missing, ask the task to list the root and select an existing document.

actions.title: Follow it on another device
actions.do: Sign in on iPad with the same account and workspace and open the same cloud task. Compare the reported heading to the repository on GitHub.
actions.see: The cloud result remains available without the desktop computer running the job.
actions.stuck: If the task is absent, compare workspaces and check whether the original task ran locally.

roles: Read documentation in an approved sample repository.
Review a source-controlled onboarding guide on a tablet.
Check an app’s README while away from the desktop.

title: Start a Work task that produces a deliverable
summary: Work can prepare a finished output from instructions and source material. Try a short handoff without attaching anything.
where: Sign in at chatgpt.com, in the ChatGPT desktop app for Mac or Windows, or in the ChatGPT app on iPad. Work availability depends on the account.

actions.title: Choose Work
actions.do: On desktop select ChatGPT in the product menu, then Work. On web choose Work. On current mobile layouts start a chat, tap the message box, then the model name and choose Work.
actions.see: The new conversation shows Work as its mode.
actions.stuck: If mobile uses the classic layout, open the Chat or Work dropdown. Check your plan or workspace if the option is absent.

actions.title: Give it the material
actions.do: Type “Write a four-line handoff. Facts: Friday, two fixtures checked, one still open, Dana owns the open item. Include owner and remaining work.”
actions.see: Work produces a short handoff you can check line by line.
actions.stuck: If it asks for a file, say the four supplied facts are the complete source.

actions.title: Correct one fact
actions.do: Reply “Replace Friday with Thursday. Keep the counts and owner.”
actions.see: The document says Thursday with two checked and one open.
actions.stuck: If it adds a deadline, point out that the source has no due date.

actions.title: Find the result later
actions.do: Return to Recents in ChatGPT and reopen the Work conversation. Check the revised result.
actions.see: You can continue the handoff in its original context.
actions.stuck: If Recents is filtered to Chat, select Work or clear the filter. Codex has its own history.

roles: Prepare a shift handoff from supplied counts.
Summarize a fictional rollout status.
Write a handoff for an app tester.

title: Create a ChatGPT project for ongoing work
summary: A project keeps related chats, sources and instructions together. This exercise needs no local folder access.
where: Use ChatGPT on the web, desktop or iPad, signed into the same account you plan to use later. Open the sidebar.

actions.title: Create the project
actions.do: Choose New project in the sidebar or the add control beside Projects. Enter Practice Handoffs and confirm.
actions.see: A new project appears by name in the sidebar.
actions.stuck: On a narrow screen open the sidebar first. If the control is absent in a managed account, check whether project creation is enabled.

actions.title: Set the project instruction
actions.do: Open the project menu, then Project settings. Enter “When making a handoff, use the headings Decision and Next step.” Save.
actions.see: The instruction is associated with Practice Handoffs.
actions.stuck: If you opened general account settings, close them and use the menu next to this project’s name.

actions.title: Start a project conversation
actions.do: Start a new chat from inside Practice Handoffs. Choose Work if offered. Ask for a handoff from “Decision: extend the trial. Next step: Lee tests on Tuesday.”
actions.see: The result uses the two requested headings and the supplied facts.
actions.stuck: Check the project name above or beside the chat if the instructions appear to be missing.

actions.title: Test continuity
actions.do: Return to the project and start a second chat. Ask for a handoff about a completed checklist and an owner who still needs to sign it.
actions.see: The second chat uses the same headings without you repeating the instruction.
actions.stuck: If only the first chat follows the pattern, confirm that you saved a project instruction instead of sending it as an ordinary message.

roles: Keep related report-writing chats together.
Keep a rollout’s approved source notes together.
Keep an app’s design and testing conversations together.

title: Attach a source and verify what Work read
summary: A source stored in a ChatGPT project can support more than one conversation. Use a tiny file with a known answer.
where: Use the Practice Handoffs project or create a new ChatGPT project. On iPad use a plain-text file already saved in Files.

actions.title: Prepare a small file
actions.do: In TextEdit on Mac choose Format → Make Plain Text, or open Notepad on Windows. Save counts.txt containing two lines: Ready 8 and Waiting 3. On iPad you can use an existing plain-text editor and Save to Files.
actions.see: You have a file named counts.txt in a known location.
actions.stuck: If no text editor is available, use the project’s paste-text source option where shown and enter the same two lines.

actions.title: Add it to the project
actions.do: Open project Sources, choose Add source or the file upload control, and pick counts.txt. On iPad use Browse in the file chooser to find it.
actions.see: The project’s source list now includes counts.txt or the pasted text source.
actions.stuck: If the file appears only as an attachment in one chat, go back to the project’s Sources area.

actions.title: Ask Work to use that source
actions.do: Start a project Work chat and request “Use the project counts. Give the two values and their total, and identify the source.”
actions.see: The expected total is 11.
actions.stuck: If the answer says it cannot find counts, check the current project and whether the upload finished.

actions.title: Check the evidence
actions.do: Open the original source and compare the result. Ask how the total would change if Waiting rose by 2, without changing the saved source.
actions.see: The hypothetical total is 13 and the original text still says Waiting 3.
actions.stuck: If the response changes Ready as well, ask it to explicitly show 8 + (3 + 2).

roles: Use a sanitized message queue count.
Use a mock rollout count.
Use sample play-test results.

title: Meet your OpenAI dot
summary: A dot is OpenAI’s persistent ChatGPT agent. It has a cloud computer and can continue work between conversations. Start with a small request that needs no connected apps.
where: Use a desktop browser, ChatGPT desktop app, or the current ChatGPT iOS app on iPad. Mobile web is unsupported. Access depends on plan, rollout, region and workspace settings.

actions.title: Find Dots
actions.do: Sign in to ChatGPT. Open Dots from the sidebar or use the Dot tab in the mobile app. Choose the option to create a dot if you do not already have one.
actions.see: Eligible accounts show onboarding or an existing dot conversation.
actions.stuck: If it is missing, confirm the correct account and workspace and check the current availability section in OpenAI’s guide.

actions.title: Identify your dot
actions.do: Follow onboarding and choose a name if prompted. Open the dot’s profile to see its identity. Leave optional app and computer connections off for this exercise.
actions.see: The named dot has its own conversation.
actions.stuck: If your profile already shows a dot, open that one. There is no need to reset it.

actions.title: Give one complete assignment
actions.do: Send “Use only these facts: room A holds 8, B holds 12, C holds 16. Recommend the smallest room for 11 people and explain your arithmetic.”
actions.see: It should recommend B because 8 is too few and 12 is enough.
actions.stuck: If it offers to search calendars, reply that these three capacities are all it needs.

actions.title: Return to the same dot
actions.do: Reopen its conversation and add “Two more people are coming. Which room now?”
actions.see: The total becomes 13 and the smallest fitting room is C.
actions.stuck: If it treats two as the total, point it to the earlier group of 11 in this conversation.

roles: Rehearse a capacity check with fabricated counts.
Track a changing planning constraint.
Keep decisions about one app feature in a continuing assignment.
sources: OpenAI · getting started with your dot

title: Give a dot a short assignment and inspect its activity
summary: Practice finding an assignment and correcting it before trying recurring work.
where: Open your existing dot in ChatGPT on desktop or iPad. The desktop profile is the clearest place to inspect activity.

actions.title: Write a clear stopping point
actions.do: Send “Draft a three-item packing check for one laptop, one charger and one adapter. Stop after posting the draft here.”
actions.see: You should see a short checklist in your conversation.
actions.stuck: If it asks to connect files, explain that the three items in your message are the entire source.

actions.title: Inspect what happened
actions.do: Select your dot’s name or avatar to open its profile. Inspect the relevant task or activity where available, then return to the conversation.
actions.see: You can distinguish the requested checklist from other dot work.
actions.stuck: For a simple reply, there may be no separate long-running task. The conversation itself preserves the response.

actions.title: Give feedback
actions.do: Say “This trip uses USB-C outlets. Remove the adapter and show the updated list.”
actions.see: The new list contains only laptop and charger.
actions.stuck: If a third item remains, ask which supplied fact requires it.

actions.title: Inspect ongoing work
actions.do: Open Scheduled in ChatGPT or the dot’s profile. This one-time exercise should not have created a recurring schedule. Identify the control used to manage an existing scheduled task without changing it.
actions.see: You can tell an ordinary follow-up apart from an actual scheduled assignment.
actions.stuck: If your dot already has other schedules, inspect their names and leave them as they were.

roles: Inspect whether a draft report was a one-time assignment.
Distinguish a task update from a recurring job.
Track small changes to a project brief.
sources: OpenAI · getting started with your dot

title: Turn a chat into a page in ChatGPT Space
summary: Make a checklist you can reopen and edit. The page holds the finished words while the conversation holds your requests.
where: Use the ChatGPT website or desktop app with a supported account. Space is for adults with eligible access. A younger reader can do the paper version with an adult.
On paper, draw a line down a sheet. Label the left side Requests and the right side Packing list.

actions.title: Gather the material
actions.do: In a new Work conversation, type “Packing list for our pretend ferry walk: hat, water, notebook.” On paper, put those words on the Requests side.
actions.see: The starting material has three items. You can count them before a page is created.
actions.stuck: If your tool opens an old conversation, start a fresh one so earlier items cannot slip in.

actions.title: Create a page
actions.do: Ask “Make a page named Ferry Packing List. Give each item its own line.” Open the resulting page. On paper, copy the three items to the right-hand side under the title.
actions.see: You now have a named page with three lines. You can edit it directly or ask for a change.
actions.stuck: If Space is missing from the sidebar, check your account and access or use the paper version.

actions.title: Make a narrow edit
actions.do: Ask to replace “water” with “water bottle” and keep the other two items. Compare the revised page with the left side of your paper or the original message.
actions.see: The middle item is more precise. Hat and notebook still appear exactly once.
actions.stuck: If new items show up, ask to restore the original three lines and change only the middle one.

actions.title: Find the result later
actions.do: Return to Space in the sidebar and reopen the page by its name. Check the wording there. On paper, fold away the Requests side and read the list.
actions.see: Someone can use the finished list without rereading the whole conversation.
actions.stuck: If you find a chat instead of the page, open the named page in Space or follow the page link inside the chat.

roles: Keep a reviewed checklist alongside a report exercise.
Turn pretend meeting decisions into an editable page.
Keep a short feature checklist in a place you can return to.
